If not, I'll wash the sheets, clean the bathroom, dust, and clean the floors during my stay, but I don't feel a need to do that for the host when I leave; that's what the cleaning fee is for. All of this is consistent with what you'd expect from housekeeping in a hotel room, adjusted for local standards and customs. comments.body: Interesting article.   I believe that drivers should have the choice to purchase whichever vehicle they feel best meet their needs.  No matter how you feel about the ICE/EV debate, it shows that the cost per mile to "fuel" your EV goes up significantly if you are not charging at home and have to use commercial DC "quick chargers" when traveling.  This is especially true since EV are less efficient at highway speeds than when in town where they can take advantage of regenerative braking.   Once the Federal government figures out how to collect the 18.4 cents tax that from EV owners that gas cars pay, it will further skew the "fuel" costs for their EV!

comments.name: Michael Welsh
comments.body:
EVs really shine when you use them for commuting and shortish trips, and can do most of your. charging at home.  The author paid between 45 and 70 cents per kWh at charging stations, but most of us pay between 12-25 cents per kWh at home.  Charging a compact EV at level 1 (120V at 12 amps, from a standard wall outlet) restores 5 or 6 miles of range per hour, so a 12 hour overnight charge will restore around 60 miles of range while consuming arround 18 kWh of power, for a cost of around $2.70, if you are ;paying $.15 per kWh.  Thus, if you are using this vehicle for commutes of less than 30 miles each way, you won’t even need a special charger.  And if your commute is a bit longer than that, you can restore full charge over the weekend.

I know a number of people who keep a large pickup or SUV for projects and long trips, while minimizing the mileage and wear and tear on it by using their EV as a daily driver and runabout for shopping, etc.  My neighbor has gone one better; if the weather is nice, he uses an E-Bike with a trailer to run to the store.

I considered buying one, did some investigation and spoke to a few owners. With all the noise about EVs, I was curious as most folks either rave about them or hate them. Here is my take:

Pros: Smooth quiet and fast. I can see where maintenance is significantly less than ICE. Definitely a differnt driving experience. 

Cons: Insurance is higher. They can also be a problem if damaged in an accident. One guy had his in the shop for +6 months waiting on parts and someone qualified to fix it.

Range anxiety for sure. I had a Tesla in Idaho in the winter and it was a constant concern. Resale is a huge issue as EVs depreciate quickly. 

Tesla's FSD should be banned from the streets. Hundreds of deaths and thousands of lawsuits tell you the story there. 

My conclusion: If you like EVs, have at it.  In my book, this technology is not ready for prime time. Its definitely not for me and I'll drive ICE for many years to come.  As long as the gooberment doesn't try to force EVs on me or subsidize purchases of EVs, I'm fine with it.

The Board has summed it well in its closing paragraphs as under:
“ In the case of Ms. Omar, the administration has gone back more than a quarter-century to investigate a prominent critic. Nice investigation of this to unpack what all had transpired here. And also, it’s important to note that the claimant did in fact get paid - a win. 

A couple of important points that might be of interest to the subject of this article as well as anyone else who is new to purchasing and using travel insurance:
1. Most trip policies that have trip cancellation protection start from the day the policy is purchased. This means that when you book those non-refundable tickets to Thailand in April for your September trip, if you break your leg or otherwise become medically unable to travel anytime before your trip, you are covered. This is why I generally buy the trip insurance policy within a few days of locking down and paying for our flights or other non-refundable items like vacation packages.

2. Regarding Generali, we’ve used them for trip insurance in the past and had to make a big claim with them when my wife tripped and broke her hip, requiring a full hip replacement. Our experience with them was excellent throughout the process. They were very responsive and helpful, going so far as to book and prepay our return flights home which needed to be business class from a different city than our original ticket was for. They were very generous in reimbursing us for every expense we incurred after her fall until we got home, and even afterwards when they paid for her followup visits with her regular doctor here.

The one thing all A.I. developers agree on is that they have no idea how their algorithms process information.  They only know that their model has weights, and through tweaking the weights through training they can force the desired results.  
In this case, the desired results are increased test scores by students after using their academic software.  

But as any teacher will tell you, it matters how students are achieving high test scores.  Are they learning to guess the most likely  correct answer on a multiple choice exam, rather than using acquired reading comprehension skills to decipher a paragraph of English literature or acquired mathematical reasoning skills to compute the correct answer to a math problem?  

Given that large language models are next-token predictors, I fear that students taught by A.I. are themselves becoming next-token predictors on exams.

I still remember the books I used in elementary school, and I'm sure you can remember each of them too.

comments.body:
Another promising educational trend that is certain to fall short and disappoint. If we want children to learn at a high level we need to consider all the factors that affect them as learners.

First is home environment. What correlates most with high-test scores is affluence. We need to ensure that all children live in safe environments where there needs are met. Cutting back on safety net programs as the Trump administration is doing is harmful to a child's cognitive development and potential. 

As for schooling, we need to focus on how children actually learn. There have been great strides in this in the area that's come to be called Mind, Brain, Education Science that considers the whole child. The neurology of learning is especially relevant. Interestingly, the findings of MBE Science supports the progressive educational approach most notably championed by John Dewey around 1900. The emotional component of learning is also paramount as has been observed by Mary Helen Immordino-Yang, professor of education, psychology, and neuroscience and founding director of the USC Center for Affective Neuroscience, Development, Learning and Education (CANDLE).

Schools also maintain entrenched methods that are ineffective, harmful, or both. For example, there is no evidence of any benefit of homework at the elementary level. But there is for reading!

I’m the principal at one of Alpha’s specialty schools.

Regarding 2x learning: 2x is our average and our target. It is true that not all of our students hit that mark. For more than 95% of students to achieve 2x learning, the average would have to be closer to 3x.

Individual parents see exactly how their child is learning relative to our goals, e.g., “This semester your child grew at 2.3x in reading and 1.7x in math.”

We hold ourselves to a strict standard and are working hard to make 2x a floor, not an average. I think we will get there. But even now most parents are pretty happy with results like these.

As for the rest: there are some fair critiques in this article, but also a number of inaccuracies. The most important is the notion that Alpha pushes students out for academic underperformance. We don’t do that. When targets are missed, it’s our fault, not the student’s. (Like many private schools, we do counsel families out in rare cases of serious behavioral problems.)

—Matt Bateman

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
Thank you, Mr. McWhorter.  

One little word (flung out as it were) caught my eye.  A disquieting little word.  

"Tribal." 

And my goodness!  Aren't we all haunted by that fear?   That we're breaking apart into tiny walled enclaves--

--angrily, obstinately cut off from other people--

--incapable of lifting our eyes, discerning the huge open spaces, the distant horizon.   

But here I was reminded of Stephen Crane.  And that Civil War classic "The Red Badge of Courage."  

Which (to be sure) Ernest Hemingway dismissed as the fantasy of a boy that'd never strayed near a battlefield.  

Okay.  Good point. 

But I've read, too, that veterans of both north and south devoured the book.  Then came the arguments.  Which side had Mr. Crane fought on?  Was he rebel or Yank? 

But the man was born--when was it?  In 1870?   Five years after the war ended. 

And does it matter?  "Red Badge of Courage" was a classic from the day it was published. 

To say nothing of Homer's Iliad.  Was Homer himself a warrior?  People have pointed out tiny blunders in his picture of Mycenean warfare--

--notably the use of chariots.  Those Greek warriors (in Homer) turn their chariots into taxi cabs--

--shades of the battle of the Marne!

They drove up.  They climbed out.  They fought on foot--

--and who cares?  After three thousand years, the Iliad remains an unforgettable picture of human warfare.  The courage, the obstinacy that impel people to take up arms.  

Thank you, Mr. McWhorter.

We do it in Word and after decades, it's thousands of pages of genre "literature" that almost no one would call literature. Is my "lived experience" sufficient to write these characters I've recent played?  Is "range" allowed?

- An innkeeper, who is also the head of a bandit gang. His gender and orientation match mine, his skin color is mildly different from mine, but his criminal career, mannerisms, speaking style, and culture aren't similar to me. My characterization was drawn from fiction, not my life.

- A bartender. Similar and different from me in the same ways as the innkeeper, except he's also a different orientation, but on the other hand like me he's not a criminal.

- A waitress. Similar coloration and I've done a similar job. But different gender - not to mention she lives in a magical medieval world.

- A wolfwere. Natural form of a male wolf.  Can take any humanoid form and was last seen pretending to be a female half-elf singer. I've been a singer, but not a shapeshifter or canine. Orientation: carnivorous.

- A common water snake. I met one in the wild in my childhood and wrote it like I remembered, well enough that two of my players guessed its species from real world encounters of their own. I never pondered its gender or orientation.

Jeanine Cummins captured the sight, sound and, yes, even smell, of the immigrant experience of trekking thousands of miles to come to this country. It was Miriam Gurba who attcked Ms. Cummins writing because she did not live the experience. Fortunately, Ms. Cummins did not have to live the horrific experience she wrote about based on research and discussion with people who did. Fiction writing is a creative endeavor and every reader should be cognizant of the perspective of the writer but ultimately consider the writing from their own perspective. I see almost no fictional characters of any race or gender who are presented as being like what is actually going on inside of my head. For the most part this doesn't bother me at all. Really the only time it's disturbing is when some character is clearly meant to illustrate what someone else assumes I must be thinking, on the basis of my race and gender. I think the problem isn't that they're getting the particulars wrong but rather the basic assumption that (race, gender) implies particular thoughts, attitudes, etc.

I think I could write about a black woman who thinks X and has attitudes Y and Z. I don't think I could write a black female character whose thoughts and attitudes reflect those of black females in general.

comments.name: Koala

Following on from my comment below but deserving its own thought box, regarding The Question of whether one can validly write of experiences not lived (in this lifetime), is this:

How often have you commented on a political article using terms such as "most Americans" or "many Americans" or "most Republicans" and so on?

Such as, "most Americans don't like that" 

What's the difference?

Aren't you in that comment doing the very same thing: casting your mind outside of your lived experiences, because you don't know most Americans, to psychically lasso experiences those people have and write about them confidently and just as though you did?

To draw on some form of wellspring, somewhere?

(I think we have to be careful here, too, to not confuse the question with 'bad writing'.)

We as humans have access to extraordinary warehouses of knowledge, including non-physically-kept knowledge, and we perform all sorts of mental skill adventures getting that knowledge quite naturally and without thinking about what exactly we're doing when we do it.

I'm using the word "knowledge" there in the sense that the knowledge is or could be common to others, but the principle works just the same if it's knowledge that is so deemed by an individual. 

At least, most mystics would think so if not most Americans, don't you think?

Beginning March 12, 1998, Six Flags Over Georgia held a roller coaster marathon.  Initially, 24 contestants rode The Great American Scream Machine continuously. The survivor would win a $16,000 Jeep Wrangler. They rode for 12 hours a day, one lap every 2½ minutes with a short break every hour.  This 12-hour-a-day roller coaster ride proceeded in the rain and cold, unless there was thunder and lightening (due to the risk of electrocution).

By March 26, Day 14, ten people were still riding The Scream Machine. These folks got a five to fifteen minute break every hour, and 45 minutes for lunch and dinner. Otherwise, they rode from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. every day, 14 hours.

On Day 22, they moved from The Scream Machine to The Georgia Cyclone, a much rougher roller coaster ride, and rode 17 hours a day, from 8 a.m. until 1 a.m. They made the contest harder hoping that some would drop out.

April 16, Day 34, Guinness Book of World Records certified the contest. The prior U.S. record of 11 days and world record of 23 days had been broken. There were only 3 contestants left. They slept  outside in sleeping bags on the coaster platform. They did not stop for Easter.

Finally, on May 11, it was over. Each of the three contestants received a 1998 Jeep Wrangler. They rode 12,456 laps – about 25,000 miles – in 60 days.

There was no long term medical study on the health effects of this contest.

From "The Sex of a Hippopotamus: A Unique History of Taxes and Accounting."

It's about the environment.

But the thing that matters is spending the hour or so of observation, quietly, and mindfully noting the falling light levels. You have to do this without lights and distractions. 

Ideally you set your alarm by the sunrise time in your area or during winter, get up and turn on lights... preferably gradually, like a sunrise.

And then, more research showed exercise ameliorates the malign effects of poor or not enough sleep.

More research: no more than 5 oz. Water in the 4 hours before bed. No food as well. Room temperature should be cool to cold. Don't sleep with animals. Don't sleep with other people if there is any chance they disturb you.

Go down the list... do all the stuff. Make substantial changes in routine, diet, habit, daily exertions, meditations, etc.

This is a joke because AI is UNPRECEDENTED. 

unprecedented
/ŭn-prĕs′ĭ-dĕn″tĭd/

adjective
1. Having no previous example.
"unprecedented economic growth."
2. Having no precedent or example; not preceded by a like case; not having the authority of prior example; novel; new; unexampled.
3. Never before seen or done, without precedent.

One cannot draw valid or valuable conclusions from the past. It’s like all the other unprecedented modern technologies that are closing in on the environment today. Plastics, pesticides…. And even if a miracle happened to find a way to remove them, where would we put it all? 8300 million metric tons (Mt) as of virgin plastics have been produced to date. (Geyer et al)

The sociological complication is that once a technology is introduced, it becomes normalized. Younger generations assume it’s safe regardless of what’s actually known about it. And it proliferates, spreading its deleterious effects rapidly. Eventually everyone sees its harm and wants it gone. comments.name: Austin H
comments.body: Since the Pumpkins’ work in the 90s is now widely beloved (including by me), and Corgan remains an active songwriter, I’m not sure why he feels he hasn’t gotten his due, unless he’s referring to the music he’s made since then. There are undoubtedly gems in that latter body of work: I liked Oceania and Monuments to an Elegy, and wish he’d rerelease 2008’s American Gothic EP. Most of this music, though, is marred by consistent, identifiable issues. His singing is placid, rarely bothering to yearn softly or wail desperately; his lyrics are indecipherable, neither visceral or heartrending; and his compositions lack dynamics, all crunchy humbucker riffage devoid of the bright streaks of color that so brilliantly set him apart from his peers. It all fails to capture the feeling so many Pumpkins fans related to and connected with, what Ian Cohen once perfectly described as “wonderful, lovestruck propulsion.” Who knows why that fire has dimmed; many artists have proved that they can rekindle it. But it’s difficult to escape the notion that it’s because, as a songwriter, Corgan has simply stopped challenging himself.

"Reinstate expired Affordable Care Act health care premium subsidies."

These subsidies were put in place in response to the COVID-19 "emergency" and were sold as addressing that emergency in some way. The COVID-19 emergency is now in the rearview mirror with COVID-19 deaths being about the same as the flu (this varies from season to season).

There is no "emergency" now and it was right to let these expanded subsidies to expire as their justification has evaporated.

For example, the cap of 400% of FPL to qualify for any subsidy was promoted and enacted by Democrats when passing the PPACA -- are they now admitting they were wrong? If so, why should they be trusted this time around? If not, what's the justification for extending raising the cap?

The nonsense of extending government handouts put in place due to "emergencies" and then retaining them ad infinitum means that prudent citizens feel compelled to resist EVERY handout justified by a short term emergency because too often those temporary handouts become permanent.

The US Government is over $40T in debt (about $115,000 for every person in the US, including those born while you were reading this). The "one way ratchet" of emergency spending must change or every future generation in the US will suffer.

There is a shift to a known strain for which novaccineis currently available.  But it was years between the first documented human cases and the first vaccine became available.  

It was contained with the same measures public health used a century ago.  Case identification, quarantine, protective wear for caregivers. Concentric isolation, contact tracking, and public education.  It took a while for fear to overcome traditional hands-on greetings, and having the womenfolk of the village do unprotected hands-on preparation of the contagious deceased for burial that became a super-spreader event.  But public education won out.

Then support for epidemic response, testing, and education was slashed. USAID was extralegally DOGE’d.  CDC budget was slashed with a focus on eliminating international disease tracking and support.    US support for the UN and it’s health measures was eliminated.  African countries still largely lack the ability to support necessary medical and public health measures.

Unfortunately the access to and uptake of those treatments have not been equitably shared globally or even within high income countries. There was a NYT article a year ago about how around half of patients in the US with advanced lung cancer don't get life-extending treatments, and I would guess at least part of this is due to misperceptions about modern cancer treatment (as well as obviously other larger, complex, systemic factors).

My grandmother had a painful course of treatment and death from cancer while receiving what I think would have been incredibly noxious chemotherapies, but today she might have continued to live in relatively good health on an oral targeted therapy or immunotherapy. I think a lot of people now getting older might not appreciate what a shift has occurred, and I think that could influence their decision-making in the event of a cancer diagnosis or even screening measures - for instance, someone might skip mammograms because they think a diagnosis is invariably leading to horrible course of chemo that they saw their elder experience, even though that would likely be far from their experience now. Of course overscreening is also a concern, but is a hard-to-impossible thing to study in real-time with the rate of new therapies and treatment strategies emerging.

What matters is the decline in the age-adjusted mortality rates, not the five-year survival rate. The latter is subject to so-called ”lead-in bias”, meaning that early detection increases five-year survival even if the patient dies at the same age and the treatment is entirely ineffective.

Thus screening can leave mortality rates unchanged even if it increases five-year survival.

Prostate cancer is a prime example. PSA screening was introduced in the 1990s, leading to a huge increase in detected incidence and treatment but only a small decline in mortality. Millions of men were probably diagnosed and treated unnecessarily. In the meantime guidelines now advise men with low-risk prostate cancer to adopt “active surveillance” instead of treatment, since the complications of treatment are significant and the mortality benefit is nonexistent.

Key problems in screening is differentiating between indolent and aggressive cancers, and reducing false positives.

The right to protest (liberté de manifester) is guaranteed by the French Constitution, and so are the right to come and go (liberté de circuler) and freedom of expression (liberté d'expression, not as extensive as "free speech"). 

The Constitution also gives the right to the State to take measures to keep public order (maintien de l'ordre). Protests do not have to be "approved" but they can be restricted. 

The normal procedure is for protest organizers to communicate their plans (date, time, protest route) to the office of the local State representative (préfecture), which can then impose changes to the route or ban the protest for specific reasons (e.g. not enough police available to ensure order). That decision can be, and often is, appealed to the local administrative court and, if needed, on to the highest court. Those decisions are made in a timely manner to ensure that the protest, if eventually authorized, can proceed. 

In addition to being of dubious constitutionality, Macron's latest decision is tone-deaf and counterproductive.
 
What is new here is that there are *blanket* bans in a number of cities even though the country is not under a State of Emergency. If the Courts let most of those bans stay, it will be a very concerning development, and a precedent that a future far-right government would happily point to. This, in addition to countless other authoritarian measures and laws already in the books.

comments.body: It’s a horrible law. The city will be coming next for your property. It’s like mandating a car owner to notify the city of intent to sell the car and wait to see if the politically connected cronies will buy it. Some of those former council members head these housing non profits. The NY Times needs to do independent research on these not for profits. I don’t see how it’s legal. What if the landlord has a lease with a commercial tenant that gives that tenant first dibs and right of first refusal? Does that not count? Read about recent stories of not for profits with hundreds of violations on properties they took over. If the tenants don’t pay their rents and the properties become distressed the not for profits will be just as bad. Furthermore, the city is not charging them property taxes under this program. I expect a lawsuit challenging the legality of forcing a property owner to go through this process.

comments.name: George
comments.body:
While this bill give non-profits a bit of a leg up to purchase distressed properties it seems to be lacking a critical requirement.

Presumably a for-profit buyer willing to take on such a property from a distressed seller has the financial wherewithal to then make the capital improvements to repair and renew the property.

If all this bill accomplishes is to move the ownership of a distressed property from the current owner to a non-profit without ensuring that necessary repairs are then undertaken how does it result in improved housing?

In the end, it would seem that this bill will not achieve the underlying aim of stemming gentrification.

Most buildings ripe for gentrification lie on the edges of nabes close to already upscale blocks.  These buildings are considered prime for redevelopment and a for-profit buyer will almost always out-bid a non-profit competitor.

In truly distressed areas where there are few if any gentrification pressures the owners of distressed properties may well look forward to finding a non-profit buyer willing to take the property off his hands.

But this then begs my initial point.  Will that non-profit buyer then have the capital funding sources to make the necessary improvements?  Or will it just transfer a troubled property to another neglectful owner?

After all, the rent roll won't rise.  So how does the non-profit find the cash to make the needed improvements?

comments.name: William Meyer
comments.body: The financing structure of law firms — in which only a lawyer can hold equity — assures an environment in which the returns of the moment are hyper-accentuated.  Grab all you can NOW.  If you work for 20 years in any other business, building shareholder value, and you get a heart attack and keel over (happens to a lot of lawyers), or just decide to retire, your shares are bought out or sold reflecting full “enterprise” value.  Closely-held and there may be some valuation and liquidity bumps, publicly-held “easy,” but you or heirs get something approaching “full value” of what you built, subject to whatever other frictions writ-large.  Die or retire in a law firm, and your equity is redeemed at a pretend “book value” in which your former fellow shareholders have every motivation to make that number as small as possible.  This system persists as a knee-jerk “ethical” rule because “only lawyers should own and control law firms” to maintain “professional independence.”  But is it really protecting anybody, clients or lawyers? More than just making people feel safe, I think the presence of officers can also have a deterring effect on any possible threat that might happen at the school.

comments.name: Faizyab
comments.body:
I think the police should not be a regular part of school life. In my own campus we have a security guard, but no officers, and our main safety measure is a simple crowd-control system that keeps students in the classroom during lunch; the guard quickly resolves minor disputes without calling the police. When a 12-year-old in Galveston was hauled to jail for standing in a hallway, it turned a simple classroom disagreement into a legal nightmare and left a cloud of fear over the whole school.

Instead of police, we should invest in trained counselors and conflict-resolution teams. Last year, our school piloted a peer-mediator program that cut "late" incidents by 30% and reduced suspensions by 20%. A calm, supportive environment is safer for learning than a courtroom.

comments.name: Kaden
comments.body:
I believe making my school safer and healthier requires more than just having police officer son campus. Schools should focus on preventing problems and making sure students feel supported, respected, and comfortable asking for help. One idea is to provide more access to counselors and mental health resources. Students sometimes deal with stress, bullying or personal problems and may not know who to talk to. Schools can solve disagreements peacefully instead of facing serious punishment immediately.

This article explains that about 4,800 children 10-13 years old were punished during 24-25 school year. The article also talks about a 10 year old boy who faced charges after kicking an assistant principal when his phone was taken away. Even though his case was dropped, his family faced thousands of dollars in legal bills, and he became anxious about school. This evidence shows that involving police in minor incidents can seriously affect students and their families. I believe officers should respond to dangerous emergencies, while smaller problems should be handled by counselors and school staff.

From my personal experience as a student, I've seen how important it is to feel comfortable around others in school. When students feel supported, they may be more willing to speak up when something is wrong. Overall, schools should balance safety with emotional support, but they also deserve chances to learn from their mistakes without being treated like criminals.

I go to a high school that is a part of a college building, so the doors to the building are always open, and anyone at any time of any age can walk in and around near the high schoolers, and most people would not have a single care. However, I do think that having open access to the building could be a safety concern since not everyone who walks in has good intentions. I believe that having security cameras, staff members monitoring the hallways, and emergency procedures in place are important ways to keep students safe. Overall I feel safe at school but I also recognize that having proper safety measures is important, even when most people don't think about them.

Unfortunately, voters are missing some key information.

Paul Krugman on Substack the other day commented, on the coverage losses from the lapsed ACA expanded subsidies:

"we’re now in the midst of an enormous healthcare disaster — a disaster that is receiving surprisingly little media coverage with, as far as I can tell, no recent articles on massive coverage losses in any of the major newspapers. I know that there’s a lot going on, but this seems odd."

There have been no recent articles on the massive coverage losses because the three major newspapers: The NYT, WSJ, WaPo have been successfully fooled by the administration.  

The monthly updates are supposed to be on a CMS page "Health Insurance Exchanges Monthly Effectuated Enrollment",  but that page was last updated 6/26/26.

The press has been outsmarted.

For example, the last released data, on 6/26/26, showing only the start of the drops, was picked up by the WSJ, in an article of that same data, entitled "Millions of Americans Drop Obamacare Plans After Withdrawal of Subsidies".

If the administration had released additional months of data due now, say on 7/26 (for March), 8/26 (for April), and 9/26 (for May) when they were due, the three major newspapers would have picked it up in an article each time.

But, the papers all missed seeing that additional data is due! 

And the public doesn't know either of the coverage losses (that would be known if the data were out) or the cover-up of holding back 3 months of data!

comments.name: David Link
comments.body:
For me, the heart of this article is this quote from Mr. Regan: "Direct democracy is just a tool that’s available to us,” he said. “I still wonder why it doesn’t get used more.”

The union movement was one of the fundamental advances to counter the obvious problems with the incentives and power of capitalism.  Laws guaranteeing workers the right to organize to negotiate for wages, hours, benefits and working conditions are the right corrective and I support them.

But what modern labor has wrought in the last 70 years or so is laws that do the unions' negotiating work for them. Minimum wage laws are one example, public sector unions another, since the state does not have the capitalist dynamic unions counter. Every public sector union victory is paid for by taxpayers, when it's  not borrowed in some way.

Mr. Regan's manipulation of California's  initiative process clarifies the bigger picture.  Our voters have sometimes supported laws that eliminate some of the hard work unions need to do. I don't think that's a good idea, but I'm only one voter.  Regan thinks otherwise, and he makes even his fellow union leaders nervous. 

The fact that union membership in this country has fallen so far, floating around 10% of US workers suggests to me that even though the union concept still has much support, their legislative efforts might be tending in the direction of putting them out of business.

comments.body: For years, Canada has had punitive tariffs and limits on dairy products from the United States, so this is not an invisible wall.  Because of this, a gallon of milk in Ontario costs about double that of a gallon of milk in Michigan.  There is also amazing artisanal cheese made in Wisconsin, but it is kept away from Canadian customers through the Supply Management System.  It would be great if consumers on both sides of the border had easy access to these products.

comments.name: Bobinette
comments.body:
I’m from Québec and have lived there all my life: we have had laws and policies enshrined into our constitution regarding our ability to be  self-sufficient economically and especially concerning food security/protecting agricultural land and water potential since the mid-70s in preparation for independence from Canada (René Lévesque’s Parti Québécois was first elected in 1976). We have also always had a stalwart pride in our produits du terroir, our ancestors’ agricultural legacy and keeping the traditional practices alive. These combined habitus’ mean we seldom purchase produce from outside the province if something local is available. I would venture to guess about 90% of available cheese here are from local fromagers, either artisanal or industrial, and the remainder are fine cheese from Europe. I do not consider “cheese products” such as Kraft singles or Cheeze Wiz to be cheese, but those are the US “cheese” we know of.

The tariffs have not changed the grocery store habits in Québec much. It’s not that we weren’t buying US products so much as we have been prioritizing Québec for decades, then only buying imported goods when discounted. The exception was certain alcohols, but again the tariffs has allowed us to reinvest and develop new a new local market to be loyal to.

I'm happy to see prairie getting its due.

I live on the Great Plains and so I have planted blue grama and buffalo grass meadow in part of my yard. The other day I saw a small skipper butterfly. It brought me delight. Both of these grasses are larval hosts for skipper butterflies. 

I've also seen a garter snake which seek out long grass like blue grama and buffalo grass to inhabit. Garter snakes (harmless to humans) would never want to inhabit a typical American lawn of Kentucky bluegrass (native to Asia not Kentucky by the way) cropped short. 

Here is a tiny love story I wrote:

Although a lifelong gardener, I had never fallen in love with a plant until I sowed blue grama and buffalo grasses.

These were the easiest plants I'd ever grown, because they belonged.  They had once covered much of the Great Plains, where I live, and were the staple of American buffalo.

Having deep roots, these grasses do well without irrigation, store carbon in soil and regrow from wildfire. They provide seeds for native birds, cover for nests. 

Some evenings, I lie in these pretty grasses and wonder if one day, they just might feed the buffalo again.

It's fans WAY overhype it as some sort of literary masterwork; it's detractors (typically people who are averse to any media containing overt depictions of sexual activity) WAY over-hate it and attempt to hold it out as some representation of the decline of western popular literature. comments.name: Mike
comments.body:
This movie is the very rare case of a movie being better than the book. The story has been criticized for falling short in comparison to the animation. For an audience raised on hobbits and talking animals, some of the fantasy elements are familiar ground. But where the story stands apart is how it shows kids and parents making hard choices with real consequences and how the film handles the topic of grief. Even as the villain was at the height of her villainy (no spoilers), I felt sorry for her, which is a testament to the screenwriter, who turned a 550 page YA novel into a movie that never felt rushed or bloated.

Speaking of, the animation... It was so smooth, an audience member raised on Rankin/Bass Christmas movies but unfamiliar with Laika might be surprised to learn the degree to which the movie is solely made with puppets. For a medium that gets its charm for “looking fake but feeling real,” Laika shows us just how far this art form can be pushed. As a lifelong stop motion fan, I saw this film as a love letter to animation (while avoiding self-indulgence).

I teared up at the end of the movie as I watched the credits, overwhelmed with appreciation for the artists who made this film over almost 20 years. Is it too cheesy to say it felt affirming of our shared humanity? In a time when artists are losing their jobs to bad art made by boring robots, may this movie be a reminder of what humans and artists can do when given the time and resources to do their thing.

comments.body: The comments do not mention the other always thrilling dimension of the Folklife Festivals: their international component, whether India or the Silk Road or Japan or various countries of Africa or Latin America… and beyond. The celebrations of American states were always wonderful, but this other aspect of the festival introduced visitors to music, foods, customs, religion, and culture of many other parts of the world. It nurtured an openness and curiosity about the rest of the world that needs to be revived and reinforced.

comments.name: Ken Rinzler
comments.body: As a cousin to the late Ralph Rinzler, a co-founder of the Festival, I feel confident in saying that he would not be happy with the battles the Smithsonian is fighting in today's political climate. He was someone who respected and promoted history as it was, not as some now wish it to be. I remember working with him to have New Jersey as the featured state in the 1983 Festival (I was working for a NJ Congressman at the time and he told me it had been a long term desire of his but he could never seem to pull it off and I responded we would make it happen.) As told to me by my late mother, he was always an independent and free thinker who, after watching the Last of the Mohicans while a teenager, thought it would be very cool to have a Mohican haircut and thus went and got one. Apparently his very conservative physician father, who later became my mom's obstetrician, did not share that assessment and was furious. Ralph would have embraced the optimism of your article, as he was a forward-thinking individual when it came to sharing cultural knowledge, but he did love having the Festival on the Mall (which was not its original location).

It was a golden age and in high contrast to the Go Go 60's of Hollywood product. Made us feel while we were attending Stuyvesant like we were psychic adventurers on the high seas of celluloid dreams - but w/ more, much more significance. The trailer of this film feels like that or brings me back. 'course after the director of Das Boot had a hit with it they brought him to Hollywood where he was forever cubby-holed to sub films. Also, before I knew anything I was attracted to Mann's books and stories: Death in Venice, The Magician et al. It was all hypnotizing - no pun intended. The film festival arena for awhile replaced Bleecker St - until it became the Jr Varsity league for the studios. (Harvey Weinstein was spawned by them until he grew drunk on his star making power). You can never recapture the innocence of youth but this film reminds me of it and a chapter in Mann's life I knew nothing about. Every line resonates with the history of that visit and what went before. (there was 1 play by Christopher Hampton - Tales from Hollywood (I think) that illuminated Mann's life in L.A. ). Those were the days is all I can say.

I think this article may present an interesting juxtaposition to the recent stories of protests and civil unrest in the country that The Times has been covering. Just yesterday, there was an article about how some people had resorted to looting luxury items possibly out of desperation during the protests and reselling them, as opposed to keeping them for their personal enjoyment. In this context, could this type of premium pet industry be viewed as one example of a manifestation of wealth inequality, capital misallocation within society, and extreme self-indulgence, potentially misplacing our humanitarian priorities?

It’s also interesting to read about how the adoption of cats is increasing rapidly and the hypothesis that links this trend to their low maintenance nature. Is it possible that many owners are looking for a substitute or a surrogate for emotional connections resembling those found in human relationships? This may be relevant in modern societies where people are increasingly feeling more isolated and lonely, yet choose not to engage in actual relationships with other people for various reasons.

Nevertheless, my understanding is that cats are smart and largely very independent creatures that are highly capable of surviving on their own. On occasion, I wonder if it is a healthy practice for some people to make cats so dependent on them, potentially just to fulfill their own emotional needs or derive personal satisfaction.

Jotting down some passing thoughts.
